The Ninth Circuit has held that it was an abuse of discretion to order limited discovery in a PSLRA suit to enable plaintiffs—who alleged claims
based upon “the disclosure of specific inside information by a specific person on a specific date and the subsequent ‘dumping’ of Rational stock on the
same date”—to identify the traders of the stock on the listed date. That discovery, in the appellate court’s view, was barred because it was needed to
sustain the sufficiency of the complaint, and the statute “requires the trial court to dismiss the complaint if it fails to satisfy the Act’s heightened
pleading standards.” The fact that the information was within defendant’s exclusive custody was, according to the court, beside the point. SG Cowen
Securities Corp. v. U.S. Dist. Court for Northern Dist. of CA., 189 F.3d 909, 912 (9th Cir. 1999). By contrast, the Southern District of New York has
lifted the discovery stay upon a finding that its operation would cause undue prejudice. See Vacold LLC v. Cerami, 2001 WL 167704, *2 (S.D.N.Y.
2001). When faced with a motion to lift a discovery stay, should the court weigh only the parties’ private interest, or also consider the public interest in
enforcement of the securities laws? See Erickson, Heightened Procedure, 102 Iowa L.Rev. 61 (2016).
3.AUTOMATIC DISCLOSURE
———
Read Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(a) and the accompanying materials in the Supplement.
———
The 1993 amendments to Rule 26(a)(1), requiring automatic disclosure of specified categories of information, were controversial
when promulgated. Justice Scalia filed a dissenting statement, joined by Justice Thomas and in part by Justice Souter, on the ground that
the proposal introduced “into the trial process an element that is contrary to the nature of our adversary system.” Amendments to Federal
Rules of Civil Procedure, 146 F.R.D. 401, 507 (1993). See Bell, Varner & Gottschalk, Automatic Disclosure in Discovery—The Rush to
Reform, 27 Ga.L.Rev. 1 (1992). Concerns also were expressed that the rule would increase cost and delay and decrease incentives to
settle. See Issacharoff & Loewenstein, Unintended Consequences of Mandatory Disclosure, 73 Tex.L.Rev. 753 (1995). In 2000, the duty

of automatic disclosure was limited to information that the party intends to use. See Huang, Mandatory Disclosure: A Controversial
Device with No Effects, 21 Pace L.Rev. 203 (2000).
In CUMMINGS v. GENERAL MOTORS CORP., 365 F.3d 944, 953–54 (10th Cir. 2004), abrogated on other grounds by Unitherm
